endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: Prior to issuing an adverse determination, the treating physician must have the opportunity to discuss the medical necessity of the care directly with the physician who will be responsible for determining if the care is authorized.

endorsements.title: FUTURE-AI: international consensus guideline for trustworthy and deployable artificial intelligence in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Accountability mechanisms should be established, incorporating both individual and collective liability, alongside compensation and support structures for patients affected by AI errors.

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether patient feedback and support channels for AI errors improve recourse, safety, or trust, and no supplied study documents the hazard. The recommendation rests on two guidance documents, one of which addresses physician-to-physician review of adverse determinations rather than patient support.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The two endorsements are expert consensus, and one addresses a related but different mechanism, so the support is indirect as well as untested.

The FUTURE-AI guideline calls for compensation and support structures for patients affected by AI errors. The Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use require that a treating physician can discuss medical necessity with the reviewing physician before an adverse determination. That provision gives clinicians a route to contest decisions but creates no channel for patients.

commentary.research_gap: No study has evaluated whether patient-facing reporting, guidance, or support channels for AI errors are used, whether they are independent of business interests in practice, or whether they lead to faster error detection, remediation, or compensation. Studies are also needed to measure how often patients experience AI-related harm and what recourse they currently seek.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems cannot yet know whether such channels would be reachable or usable for these patients, who may face language, literacy, and access barriers to filing complaints.
